Atsuge

Also find this entry through: Atsuge — historical Hat Creek grouping

Atsuge is a historical Hat Creek regional name within Atsugewi accounts. This entry follows place, named cultural teachers and the limits of historical scholarship, while linking to living Pit River communities today. It is not an additional modern band count or a claim that descendants disappeared.

Read the sources [1] Lassen Volcanic National Park, National Park Service [2] National Park Service [3] Thomas R. Garth / University of California Press, Anthropological Records 14(2),129–212

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

A Hat Creek name in context

The National Park Service distinguishes the Atsuge of Hat Creek Valley from the Apwaruge farther east in its Atsugewi account. Garth’s 1953 study uses the same regional distinction, based on fieldwork in 1938 and 1939. These are historical and interpretive categories. The Tribe’s modern constituent-band names and present membership cannot be reconstructed simply by equating each older name with a current roll.

Read the sources [1] Lassen Volcanic National Park, National Park Service [3] Thomas R. Garth / University of California Press, Anthropological Records 14(2),129–212

02

Named teachers and public cultural work

NPS records Selena LaMarr’s basketry and acorn-processing demonstrations beginning in 1952, later joined and continued by other named cultural teachers. The accompanying archival picture identifies her with Hat Creek Atsugewi basketry. It is one person’s public cultural work, not an image of every modern band member. The park’s account also describes tribal participation in collections and interpretation, making continuing community involvement visible.

Read the sources [1] Lassen Volcanic National Park, National Park Service [2] National Park Service

03

Reading historical basketry accounts carefully

Garth names Atsuge contributors and interpreters rather than providing an anonymous cultural inventory. His selected basketry discussion records Sarah Brown’s recollection of learning a coiling technique from a Maidu friend. That is an attributed personal account of learning and exchange, not proof of one origin for all basketry. His period judgments, population estimates and predictions about cultural loss are not adopted as present facts.

Read the sources [3] Thomas R. Garth / University of California Press, Anthropological Records 14(2),129–212

What needs further research

  • Compare community-authored preferred naming with dated historical scholarship; pasted ChatGPT essay is a lead, not verification.
  • Do not silently add Atsugé/Astuge spelling variants from the pasted essay without an inspected source.
  • Existing selected reviews are transferred with original dates/scopes; a short route is not a full reading of every underlying work. No present census, band-roll equivalence or community endorsement.

Atsugewi Ethnography — selected historical passages ↗

Publication: 1953-02-27

Selected 1938–1939 fieldwork account names contributors and interpreters, distinguishes Hat Creek and Dixie Valley settings, and records Sarah Brown’s account of learning basket coiling from a Maidu friend. Its period judgments and disputed geography remain attributed to Garth, not present-day community definitions.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual 90-page primary PDF downloaded; title/imprint and contents checked; contributor list PDF 5; printed 129–131(PDF 8–10); printed 148–151(PDF 27–30), basketry subsection specifically. Printed 150 visually verified from a rendered page. Other chapters, plates and ceremonial/medical sections not closely reviewed or used.

Review recorded: October 30, 2026

Access note: Catalogue normal web request 403, stopped. The openly indexed primary PDF itself returned 200 and its offered redirect was followed normally, not by altered headers or a fabricated rendition. Fieldwork dates 1938(two months) and 1939(three weeks); publication issued February 27,1953. Salvage-era assumptions, subjective ratings of speakers, population estimates, ritual instructions, curing recipes and allegations about neighboring peoples are not adopted. No legal-boundary or modern-roll inference. A narrator’s account of introducing coiling is not a proven unique origin for every basket.

https://digicoll.lib.berkeley.edu/record/84175/files/ucar014-003.pdf
